refsect1.title: DESCRIPTION
refsect1.para:
This manual page is an overview of how runlevels are used with
vera 8 .

The term runlevel dates back to the original UNIX init process supervisor. At a given time the system is in one of several pre-defined runlevels. The runlevels determine which major system processes are running. The original runlevels were single characters, vera uses more descriptive labels and understands the legacy single-character runlevels as their aliases:

row.entry: Custom (same as multi-user), network enabled in some systems
Target started in response to vera receiving a SIGINT signal
Target started in response to vera receiving a SIGPWR signal, depending on the contents of /etc/powerstatus
Target started in response to vera receiving a SIGHUP signal
Target started in response to vera receiving a SIGWINCH signal
On-demand targets, start by vlad start system/LETTER

refsect1.para: The actual behavior and environment of each runlevel depends on how the system is configured. It's also possible to define new runlevels (see for more information). The switch command takes an argument and changes the system runlevel, for example: vlad switch reboot reboots the system. vera recognizes legacy runlevel aliases, vlad switch 6 has the same result.

For compatibility with init, a single parameter to vlad consisting of a single letter or digit gets interpreted as a reference to an init runlevel, an ondemand action, or an inittab update, and triggers the equivalent command. vlad 6 also triggers a reboot.
switch does not wait for all processes to stop and start and returns immediately. The --wait option makes switch wait until the switch to the new runlevel finishes.
current shows the current runlevel. The default command shows the default runlevel when the system starts. Passing a parameter to default changes the default system startup runlevel.

note.para: vlad default runlevel sets the default runlevel for the next system boot. vera does not read the default runlevel until it gets started or restarted; but the default runlevel has no other function except to set the runlevel when the system boots.

refsect1.para: The --override option sets a "temporary" override for the default runlevel. The override gets removed by the next set default. The previous default gets restored by setting a default of default:

informalexample.programlisting: # vlad default graphical # Current default runlevel is graphical # vlad default multi-user # vlad default multi-user # New default # vlad --override default graphical # vlad default graphical # vlad default default # vlad default multi-user # Reverts to the previous default runlevel

refsect2.title: System runlevels
refsect2.para: The file @RUNLEVELCONFIG@ defines system runlevels. A default one gets installed and it should only be updated by vlad.

This file is a YAML document, a map. The map keys are the canonical names of predefined runlevels. The map values are lists of aliases for each runlevel. Exactly one of the map keys have an alias called default, this is the default system runlevel. The vlad default command updates this alias by rewriting the configuration file.

vera automatically creates internal units for runlevels' canonical names. Additional unit specification files get installed in @INSTALLCONFIGDIR@/system, for each runlevel. These system units, like system/graphical and system/multiuser, are the ones that are referenced by enabled dependencies (see ).

listitem.para: Runlevel configuration, for compatibility with sysvinit.
